https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-forei.text: Paris and Berlin have thrown their weight behind a call to make EU decision-making on foreign policy and security more efficient, according to a letter seen by POLITICO. In the letter, addressed to High Representative Kaja Kallas and signed by 11 EU states including France and Germany, the signatories spell out five ways to boost the speed and efficiency of decision-making in common foreign and security policy (CFSP), including potentially increasing the use of qualified majority voting. Under EU rules, decisions that fall under a CFSP heading must be approved unanimously by all 27 EU countries — a rule that caused major bottlenecks when former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán repeatedly used his veto to block decisions backed by all 26 other capitals. Advertisement Advertisement Germany, in particular, has led calls to move from unanimity voting on CFSP to so-called qualified majority voting (QMV), but France, among other states, has traditionally opposed such a change. The letter opens the door to greater use of QMV without explicitly endorsing any wholesale change in voting methods. "We continue to strive for consensus wherever possible," reads the letter signed by the foreign ministers of Austria, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Belgium, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain in addition to France and Germany. " But we must also ensure that this culture of consensus fosters common action rather than preventing it — otherwise we will have legitimacy but no strength." The steps outlined in the letter are: Emphasizing the principle of "sincere cooperation" between EU states — meaning that countries must honor commitments they have made to one another, even if they are not strictly legally binding. Using "constructive abstentions" rather than outright vetoes, "so as not to prevent the Union from acting." Banning linkage of "unrelated matters" to an issue being debated — or cracking down on the practice of holding collective decisions hostage by threatening a veto unless the others agree to a separate national demand. Encouraging the EU's chief diplomat, currently Kaja Kallas, to explore treaty-based options to improve decision-making. The treaty-based option most commonly invoked is the so-called Passerelle clause, which allows the EU to change decision-making rules without changing any treaties — for example, to allow QMV voting on specific foreign and security policy matters. Emphasizing the need to spell out the reasons why a country invokes its veto rights for "vital and stated reasons of national policy," namely when a decision is taken by qualified majority. The letter is due to be discussed this week as foreign ministers gather in Wicklow, Ireland for informal talks in the Gymnich format. Those talks will also explore options for reforming the European External Action Service, the EU diplomatic branch headed by High Representative Kallas. According to a Franco-German letter seen by POLITICO, options for reforming the EEAS include making Kallas an executive vice president of the European Commission with "de facto" oversight of external-facing policy units as regards trade, development aid and defense; and embedding much of the EEAS's staff inside the Commission in a new department for external relations. Staff focused on security and defense policy would remain in the EEAS, and the ratio of one-third of EEAS staff being seconded diplomats from EU states would be maintained in this new unit. The discussion paper also emphasizes the role of EU states in shaping foreign policy, envisaging a formal role for the High Representative to report to EU leaders on foreign policy matters and receive instructions directly from them during European Council gatherings. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27925.text: Big News Network.com Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant restarts Unit 3 as Danube water level rises BUDAPEST, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant restarted Turbine 6 of Unit 3 on Saturday as emergency construction measures and rising water levels in the Danube River improved cooling conditions, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said. Turbine 6 of Unit 3 was taken offline earlier this month after record-low water levels in the Danube severely restricted the amount of cooling water that could be drawn from the river. Located about 100 km south of Budapest, Paks has four VVER-440 reactor units with eight turbines in total, normally generating around half of Hungary's electricity. Its four reactors rely on water from the Danube for cooling. At the end of July, falling water levels forced the plant to sharply reduce production, with only one turbine remaining in operation at the lowest point of the crisis. Improving conditions allowed a second turbine to resume production on Aug. 10. "If everything goes according to plan, the nuclear power plant will reach its nominal capacity of 2,000 megawatts by Wednesday, and one month after the first turbine was shut down, all eight turbines will once again be in operation," Magyar said during a live broadcast from the plant on Saturday evening. The government last week ordered emergency measures to secure the plant's cooling-water supply, including the construction of a submerged weir on the Danube between Paks and Dunaszentbenedek and the controlled sinking of two 80-meter barges across part of the river. Magyar said Wednesday that the partially completed weir and the two barges had already raised the water level at the plant by around 15 centimeters, helping keep the two turbines then in operation running despite critically low water levels in the Danube. https://praguemonitor.com/work-life/how-.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points There is no single national application: each faculty sets its own deadline, fee, entrance test and document list, usually published a year ahead. A foreign secondary-school certificate has to be recognised as equivalent before study, and the university tells you whether it handles this itself or sends you to a regional office. Documents from abroad often need an apostille or legalisation and a sworn translation, which can take weeks. On this page 8 sections One faculty, one process What the faculty asks for Recognition of your certificate Entrance exams and tests Language proof A hypothetical timeline Fees and money After the offer The best advice for an applicant to a Czech university is the least glamorous: begin a year early, and begin with the paperwork. The entrance test is the part people worry about, but the papers are what kill an application. A certificate that needs an apostille, a translation and recognition cannot be produced in a week. A Czech application is not one application. There is no central clearing house that sorts applicants into places, and each faculty runs its own. That has consequences for how you plan. One faculty, one process For each programme, the faculty publishes the conditions for admission: the number of places, the closing date, the application fee, the form of entrance procedure, the documents needed and the date of results. You apply directly, typically through an online application system, and you pay a fee. You can apply to several faculties, even at the same university, which means several fees and several sets of dates. Deadlines vary. Many bachelor's programmes close for applications in the first months of the calendar year, though some fields, such as medicine, close earlier, and others later. English-language programmes for international students sometimes have separate, earlier dates. Do not trust a deadline from a previous year. Look at the faculty's page and check twice. A typical application year for a September start A year before Choose programmes, check language and recognition requirements Autumn Order apostilles and translations; prepare for language tests Winter and spring Submit applications by each faculty's deadline Spring and summer Entrance exams or interviews; results Summer Enrol, then apply for the residence permit What the faculty asks for The list differs, but you can expect most of the following. An application form, usually online. A copy of your secondary-school leaving certificate and transcript, and for a master's, your bachelor's diploma and transcript. A translation, if the documents are not in Czech, English or a language the faculty accepts. A motivation letter or CV for some programmes. Proof of language: a Czech certificate for a Czech-taught programme, or an English certificate for an English-taught one. Passport details. The application fee payment. The faculty may also ask for an apostille on the documents. An apostille is a certificate that confirms the authenticity of a public document under the Hague Convention, and a country that is not part of it may require a longer chain of legalisation. See apostille or legalisation of documents for Czechia for how that works. Translations are done by sworn translators; see sworn translations in Czechia . Recognition of your certificate If your previous education took place abroad, it normally has to be recognised in Czechia before you can study. The process is called nostrification. For foreign secondary school certificates, the body that recognises them is the regional authority ( krajský úřad ), which in Prague is City Hall. A public university can also assess a foreign secondary education for the purposes of its own admission procedure. Ask the faculty which route applies to you, because it depends on the country of the certificate and on the university. Some applicants have to go through the regional authority first, which adds weeks. Higher education diplomas follow a different path: universities, not regional offices, handle them. A bachelor's degree from abroad, if you are applying for a master's, is assessed by the university as part of admission, and a formal recognition of the degree may be needed later, for example for a regulated profession. Our guide to recognition of foreign diplomas in Czechia explains the options. Ask for the process in writing, with the expected time, and start it as early as the rules allow. Entrance exams and tests Many programmes include an entrance examination. Its form depends on the field. Typical formats are a written test in the subject, a general aptitude test, a test of languages, a portfolio for arts and design, a practical or physical test for sport and an interview. Some faculties accept results from standardised tests set by external providers in place of their own exam. Others run their own. For international applicants, the exam is sometimes held remotely or at a partner centre abroad. Check whether the faculty offers this and what proctoring arrangements it requires. If you must come in person, you need to plan travel, and if you are a visa-requiring national, you may need a short-stay visa for the exam itself. Past papers are often published on the faculty's website. Use them. Practising on old papers shows you the format and the pace. Applying to a Czech university Pick programmes and read the admission page Note the deadline, the fee, the language and the form of the entrance procedure. Start your documents Certificate, transcript, passport, language proof. Order apostilles and translations if needed. Ask about recognition Ask the faculty whether it recognises your certificate itself or sends you to a regional authority. Submit the online application Upload the documents requested and pay the fee. Keep the confirmation. Prepare for the entrance procedure Use past papers and check whether it is online or in person. Accept the place and enrol Follow the enrolment instructions, then start your residence application. Language proof For English programmes, universities usually accept internationally recognised English certificates and sometimes their own tests, with a minimum level that depends on the programme. If English was the language of your previous education, ask whether that counts. For Czech programmes, the faculty will want to see that you can follow lectures, at a level the faculty sets, shown by a certificate or a test. Many universities run preparatory Czech courses for international students, usually lasting an academic year, and some arrange admission to a degree after completion. For options, see Czech language exams for foreigners . A hypothetical timeline Take a hypothetical applicant from outside the EU who wants to start a bachelor's programme in English in September. In the autumn of the year before, they shortlist three programmes, discover that one of them requires recognition of the school certificate through a regional office and start that process at once because it can take weeks. In winter they order an apostille from their home country and a sworn translation in Czechia, which the faculty will accept. In spring they submit all three applications, pay three fees and sit an online test for two of them. In early summer they receive an offer from one faculty, and in July they book the embassy appointment. The one step that could not wait was the recognition. The test was the easy part. Missing a September start is far more often a paperwork problem than a grades problem, because every step in the chain has a waiting time. Counting backwards from the term date, and allowing for slack at every step, is the plan that works. Fees and money Application fees are charged per application and are generally not refunded if you are rejected. The amounts vary. Budget for the fee for each faculty, for translations and apostilles, for postage or courier and for any exam travel. In total the paperwork can cost more than people expect, and it is better to know in advance. Once you have a place, tuition for English-taught programmes is separate; see Czech higher education for international students . After the offer An acceptance letter is the document you need for the residence application. Without it, the embassy cannot process a student application. The letter should state the programme, the length and the start date. Keep it safe. If the university needs a deposit or the first tuition instalment before issuing a confirmation of study, check the deadline. Then see student visas and residence in Czechia for the next step, starting well before the course begins because consular appointments can take months in some countries. Do not wait for the result to start the visa chain Documents, translations and appointments take longer than the exam. Prepare the file for your residence application while you wait for your result. Frequently asked questions Is there a national application system? No. Each faculty has its own process, deadline and fee. Do I need to pass an entrance exam? Many programmes require one, but the form varies. Some use external test results or interviews. Do I need an apostille on my certificate? Often yes, depending on the country that issued it. The faculty can tell you. Can I apply to more than one faculty? Yes. Each application carries its own fee and its own deadline. Choose one programme and write its closing date, fee and document list on a single page today. Then work backwards from the date. This is a general explainer, not legal or tax advice.
